newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria posts $2.2 bln trade surplus for 9 months.
newsitem.headline: Algeria posts $2.2 bln trade surplus for 9 months.

text.p: Algerian authorities, benefiting from higher crude oil prices and early fruits of economic reform, reported on Tuesday a $2.23 billion trade surplus in the first nine months of 1996.
This compared with a $1.13 billion deficit in the same period last year.

Trade Minister Bakhti Belaib told a cabinet meeting in Algiers the performance was achieved thanks to a 19 percent fall in imports and more than 25 percent increase of the value of oil and gas exports.
The trade data and cabinet meeting was reported by the official Algerian news agency APS.

It was believed to be Algeria's highest trade surplus in a decade and came 10 days before the North African country's 13 million eligible voters decide on a draft constitution, the second time within a year they have gone to the ballot box.

Algerian authorities, locked in conflict with Moslem fundamentalists whom it blames for economic sabotage totalling more than $2 billion, are also switching the economy from nearly three decades of centralised control to a free market.

"The encouraging situation of the foreign trade balance invites more efforts in order to improve the country's financial capacities. In fact, if there is one major conclusion to be drawn from this result, it would be indeed that the challenge of the country over all fronts is within grasp," said Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia.
Imports, mainly foods and industrial spare parts, shrank by 19 percent to $6.67 billion in the first nine months of this year from $8.2 billion in the same period last year.

Oil and gas sales abroad -- 94.4 percent of exports -- rose 25.6 percent, and other exports soared 47 percent in the first three quarters of the year compared to the same period last year, Belaib was quoted saying in a government statement.
The gas and oil exports, boosted by crude price peaks in the past months, were at $8.49 billion against $6.76 billion in the same nine months last year, said the statement.
More than 59 percent of the trade surplus was achieved with Italy, which jumped as the first buyer of Algeria goods because of 24 billion cubic metres annual gas sales there.

The United States was the second largest trader with Algeria followed by France, Spain and the Netherlands. France still provided most of Algeria's imports, producing a trade deficit with France of $564 million in the first nine months of 1996 against a $955 million deficit in the same period of 1995.
Algeria, aiming to quadruple its non-oil and gas exports to $2 billion by 2000, increased by 47 percent its non-hydrocarbons exports in the first nine months of 1996 to $506 million.
"The results obtained, though still modest, showed through the steady increase of non-oil and gas exports, that the aim of $2 billion by 2000 is a perfectly reasonable possibility," said Ouyahia.

The government, improving its tax collection, gained 2.39 billion dinars ($43.4 million) from customs duties in the first nine months of the year compared to only 200 million dinars ($3.6 million) in the previous period.
The authorities allocated 10 percent of the imports customs tax, 239 million dinars, to foster non-oil and gas exports in the first three quarters of this year, the government said.
